It wasn't worth posting on LinkedIn this week. Why?

Because I've been rather busy doing the actual work. 😂

Here's what happened this week:

- Ultra-focused on my new MD role at Sixteen Eleven. 🤘

- Several new leads progressing and 2 new clients at the contract stage. 😎

- Developed invoicing and financial tracking systems so we barely have to touch those repetitive tasks again. I'd rather we spend that time doing the actual work for our clients.

- Developing media coverage tracking and reporting systems so we can capture results, measure success and demonstrate the value we're delivering across our client accounts.

- Preparing a PR strategy and pitch deck for an exciting brand within a major retail group. Fingers crossed! 🤞

- Looking to finalise a little co-working space for me and Pete. 😉❤️

- New client contracts and processes in place to protect the business and make everyone's expectations clear from day one.

- Preparing my final sessions with Boon Brown Architects, who now have a much more structured way of identifying, prioritising and developing new-business opportunities.

- Working with Abigail on CRM, AI agents and how to spot companies showing signals that they might be preparing for their next project. Rather than waiting for the brief, they can now see where opportunities might be developing. 😉🔥

And a rather long to-do list, including developing our network of specialist talent and partners to support client campaigns and events when needed. Something right up my street! ✨

Not bad for a week!

I'm still figuring out how my LinkedIn content will evolve with this new chapter, but I'll certainly keep sharing what I'm learning about running and growing businesses, building relationships and using technology to make our work easier.

And for the architecture and design studios in my network, particularly those struggling with hiring or finding the capacity to grow, I think there's a huge opportunity to use technology and AI to take some of that pressure off. You don't necessarily need more hands for every new opportunity. Sometimes you need better systems and a smarter way of working.

Anyway, time to finish a few things off and get ready for a lovely dinner with a very special friend before recharging my batteries for next week.

Happy Friday everyone! ❤️

If owning things matters more in the age of AI, the obvious question is: how do regular people get a piece of the companies building the future?

This matters more now than ever because companies stay private much longer. A generation ago, great companies went public early, and anyone with a brokerage account could buy in while they were still growing. Today the best companies can stay private for a decade or more and reach enormous valuations before the public ever gets a chance. By the time you can buy the stock, most of the growth has already happened. If you want to own a piece of the future, you increasingly have to find a way in while it's private.

The best way is still to work there. Employees get equity, a front-row seat and a real stake in the outcome. If you can get a job at a company you believe in, take the equity seriously and understand what you're getting.

But not everyone can be an employee. I wasn't one. For years, I asked to be paid in equity instead of cash, mostly for helping companies find great people. Some of it turned into something. Plenty went to zero. Here are ways I've done it, and ways I've seen others do it:

Trade your skill for equity.
Recruiting, design, legal, PR, sales, engineering on a contract. Offer to take part or all of your fee in equity. The best founders like it, because it means you're betting on them too.

Become an advisor.
If you can genuinely help with hiring, intros, fundraising or expertise, companies often grant small advisory stakes. The key word is genuinely. Show up and do the work.

Invest small.
Many founders take small checks from people who bring something besides money. Angel syndicates and SPVs let you invest alongside others with smaller amounts.

Be a scout.
Some venture firms pay scouts a share of the returns for finding great companies early.

Be an early customer or design partner.
Companies sometimes offer equity or warrants to customers who commit early and help shape the product.

Now, to founders: please make this easier.

Set aside a small equity pool for people who aren't employees. Contractors, early users, creators, advocates, the people who introduce you to your first big customer. Even a single share can turn a fan into an owner.

It's not just generous. It's brilliant marketing. People talk about what they own. An owner defends you in the comments, sends you their friends and sticks around through the bad quarters. Airbnb set aside shares for its hosts when it went public. More companies should think that way, and much earlier, especially if you plan to stay private for years.

AI is going to create enormous value, and more of it than ever will be created before companies go public. The question is how many people get to own a piece of it.

If you're building something, find a way to share it. If you believe in something, find a way to own it.

I’ve spent over 20 years in regulated environments, and I’ve learned that the biggest risks rarely arrive with a warning label. They arrive as a shortcut that makes someone’s Tuesday easier.

Right now, that shortcut is AI.

This infographic was shared with me recently, and it describes what I keep seeing. (Fair warning: it has a few typos and garbled words here and there. Please look past those and focus on the substance.) People aren’t being reckless, they’re being resourceful. They paste a contract into a free chatbot because they’re up against a deadline, not because they want to cause a breach. The figures it cites are sobering: roughly two-thirds or more of employees using tools nobody approved, and around 71% pasting sensitive data into public AI.

Smaller firms feel this most. Fewer controls, thinner safety nets, and the same liability. Courts are already treating what a company’s chatbot says as the company’s own statement.

What I like about the guidance is that it doesn’t start with “ban everything.” It starts with a simple traffic-light model:
🟢 Green: approved tools for everyday, low-risk work
🟠 Amber: check and authorise first (customer-facing content, agents that can send emails or touch files)
🔴 Red: never (credentials, confidential files, AI alone deciding hiring, pay or access)
And one principle I’d put on every wall: you own what you ship. AI can draft. A human is accountable.

The 5-day adoption plan is realistic, too: find out what’s really being used, provide sanctioned tools, write a short plain-English policy, enforce the basics (MFA, access controls), then brief the team and get sign-off. None of it needs a big budget. It needs a decision to start.

In my experience, governance works when it makes the safe route the easy route. People follow the path of least resistance, so build that path.

If you run or advise a small business, what’s one AI rule you’d want in place by Friday?

Work doesn’t stay the same shape for long any more, and the team doing it needs to be able to change with it.

The World Economic Forum’s Future of Jobs Report 2025 found employers expect 39% of their people’s core skills to change by 2030.

A permanent team built around today’s work can’t change that fast. Hiring takes time, and every permanent hire is a bet that the need will still be there in two years.

The safer bet is a mix. Keep a permanent core team that knows your business inside out, and add a liquid layer of specialists you can bring in and scale back as the work changes. Our clients often sit at around 70% permanent and 30% liquid.

That’s the Liquid Workforce™. It brings together your permanent team, the liquid layer and AI doing the jobs it’s good at, all planned as one system.

What that gives a business:

↳ Faster adaptation. Skills and team structures move when the market or the technology moves, instead of catching up after the fact.

↳ AI readiness. AI tools and automation are planned into how the work gets done and who does it, rather than bolted on later.

↳ Strategic flexibility. You set the balance between your permanent core and your liquid capacity, so you keep control without carrying cost you don’t need.

↳ Higher return on skills spend. The right expertise arrives when the work needs it and steps away on two weeks notice when it’s done, so you only pay for skills while they’re earning their keep.

↳ A workforce that keeps up. Capability grows and changes as the business does, without a restructure every time.

Brightbox works with organisations to design their Liquid Workforce and the operating model behind it. Then we resource it, with pre-vetted specialists across 15 countries on one UK contract.

So when the work changes shape, the team can change with it.

Hiring in 2026: A Short Play in Three Acts 🎭

Act 1: The Application
My AI-written resume walks into an AI-powered ATS.
ATS: "Wow. You're exactly what I was trained to look for."
Resume: "I know. I was trained to be exactly what you were trained to look for." 💅

Act 2: The Interview
The candidate's AI whispers the perfect answer about "leveraging cross-functional synergies."
The employer's AI scores it 9.4/10 for authenticity. 🤖🤝

Act 3: The Offer
Both bots agree on a salary, sign the contract, and book onboarding.
Meanwhile, the actual human is still trying to reset their LinkedIn password. 😂 🤪 

Curtain falls. Nobody claps, because nobody was in the room. 🎬

After 18+ years in HR, I'm all for tools that save us time. But I didn't sign up to be the audience at my own hiring process.

AI can sort a pile of 500 CVs. What it can't tell you is who'll stay late to help a teammate, who can calm down a furious client, or who just needs one real chance to prove themselves. That part still needs a human with good instincts and a strong cup of karak. ☕

So, recruiters and job seekers, tell me: is AI making hiring better, or just faster at being impersonal? 👇

(Asking now, before my profile starts attending interviews without me.) 🫠

KreditBee is hiring a Principal Engineer, and we'll be upfront: this is one of the hardest engineering jobs in Indian fintech right now.

The role is to re-architect KreditBee's core engineering services and build the foundation for an AI-native lending company.
That doesn't mean bolting a chatbot onto an API. It means redesigning a live, regulated, high-volume lending platform so that AI agents and humans can both work on it safely, correctly and with every action auditable, without pausing the business while we do it.
The whole design rests on one principle: clear domain separation, with exact contracts between domains.
Each domain owns its data and behaviour. Every interaction crosses a precise, versioned, testable spec: APIs, events, schemas, invariants and failure semantics, written down rather than assumed. When contracts are exact, teams move independently, migrations become safe, and AI agents can act on the system without guessing.

What that looks like day to day:
 → Drawing domain boundaries that will hold for years, not quarters
 → Writing contracts precise enough to generate code, tests and agent tools from
 → Ledger-grade correctness across distributed services
 → Migrating live money flows with zero tolerance for silent data errors
 → Deterministic guardrails around probabilistic AI components

What I actually built: • Seasonal Agriculture Performance Analysis — Cleaned and analyzed 4,000+ farm-level records across Kharif, Rabi, and Zaid seasons. Built retention recommendations around those specific behaviors. • GenAI-assisted reporting — Used AI to speed up documentation, but kept the analytical judgment (and QA) strictly human. Learning where automation helps vs. where it hallucinates was a skill in itself.
The reality check: I walked in knowing Python syntax. I walked out knowing how to handle messy, inconsistent real-world data where columns have weird names and missing values aren’t just "NaN"—they’re business problems.

Why you can't find job for 6 months? 
And why a gasoline deal can be a good thing for your career.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗶𝗻  ⛓️ 

Costs rise. Brent is around $114 a barrel, roughly 70–87% above a year ago, and US diesel is  $6+ a gallon, a record. Freight and production run on diesel, so goods get more expensive before they reach a shelf. This caused US inflation to rise to 3.7% in September. The Fed sees it and holds at 3.75–4.00% and may raise again in December. 

Companies see thinner margins, expensive credit and unpredictable demand. The first reaction is a hiring freeze. Not layoffs, just "we're not hiring".

Venture funds cannot show returns to their investors, so they push portfolio companies: cut costs or there is no next round. Public companies hear the same from analysts on earnings calls. Then comparison kicks in. If a competitor cut staff and you did not, your investors ask why. Layoffs become normal because everyone does them, not because each one is rational.

The pressure moves down the chain. A client tells its vendor "we have less to spend". The vendor has fixed costs and cannot just lower the price, so it cuts its team. An outsourced studio loses a contract and its developers and designers enter the market.

The market is also expectations. When everyone knows people are searching, interviews stretch, offers shrink or even freeze, and employed people start looking "just in case". That adds supply, which lengthens searches, which adds more anxiety.

𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗮 𝗽𝗲𝗼𝗽𝗹𝗲 𝗳𝗲𝗲𝗹 𝗶𝘁 𝗺𝗼𝗿𝗲  🚂 

When growth stalls, companies stop investing in measuring growth. It may sound paradoxical, but during a crisis, analytics is the first thing to be cut—because it doesn’t generate revenue directly; instead, it provides insight, and in a state of panic, insight can seem like a luxury.

Titles blur. Analyst, analytics engineer, data engineer and data scientist advertise overlapping but different jobs, so one search spreads across mismatched postings. Every hiring manager now has to justify a seat against "can tooling and AI cover part of this?"

𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗺𝗲𝗮𝗻𝘀  🤔 

 💡 If you're searching, fix what you control: show one business impact from your data work

 💡 If you are hiring, remember the pool in front of you is larger than usual, and the person across the table is probably tired

Mind the small print

A global electric behemoth has one cybersecurity policy and a great many suppliers. Every contract those suppliers sign ends up, sooner or later, with a cyber security team that is short of people and long on clauses. Each clause must be accepted, rejected or escalated. Multiply that by hundreds of contracts and the arithmetic turns unkind.

The usual remedies are hiring, which is slow, or skimming, which is dangerous. 

A third is to give the reviewers a capable first reader. 

That is what Contract Risk Radar does. It checks each clause against the 133 obligations in the policy and proposes one of five verdicts: accept, modify, replace, reject or escalate. Crucially, it shows its working. Each verdict comes with a reason, the contract clause it read and the policy clause it relied on, so reviewers audit an argument rather than build one from scratch.

Machines that are confidently wrong are a familiar hazard. This one is built to know its limits: when unsure, it escalates, and says why.

Confidentiality meant it was measured on synthetic contracts made to resemble the real thing. It now reads the real thing.

Buyers of such tools tend to ask how accurate they are. The better question is what they do when they do not know.

Identify the repetitive task consuming the most time.

4. Keep humans in control.

5. Measure the results.

Track time saved, quality, cost, and business impact before scaling.

The biggest mistake?

Buying AI tools before understanding the problem.

Stop pausing your search for companies that put you on hold

A recruiter tells you that you are the top finalist, but the decision is on hold.

You pause your job search. You check your inbox every hour. You convince yourself an offer is coming once leadership figures things out.

I get why you wait. You put weeks into multiple rounds of interviews. You do not want to start over from scratch.

Treat every pause as a no.

"On hold" is corporate code for cold feet. Companies freeze hiring because bosses hunt for a mythical unicorn. They want one worker who does three jobs for entry pay. They would rather drown their current team than hire a real human.

When a company wants you, they sign you before anyone else can. When they stall, they bet that you have zero other options.

Protect your own timeline:
1. Submit new applications the same day an employer tells you a role is paused.
2. Send one polite note to leave the door open, then write the job off.
3. Keep interviewing with other teams until a written contract is fully signed.

You wouldn’t hire a person who was never interviewed, tested, or checked.

So why are we hiring AI agents that way? 🤔

Most agent leaderboards show one number. It tells you almost nothing about whether an agent will survive your actual work.

At Threadpool, we're building a calibration system for AI agents of any kind: open-source models, Sarvam-powered workflows, or bring-your-own endpoints. Before an agent gets hired for a step, it earns its place through 5 layers:

🔒 L0: Gate. Is it safe? Does it stay in budget, resist prompt injection, and say “I couldn’t verify this” instead of making up a citation? Fail here and it’s never listed.

🧰 L1: Core agentic. Tool use, browsing, multi-step reasoning (GAIA, τ-bench, BrowseComp).

🎯 L2: Capability. Tested only on what it claims to do. 167 capabilities, from financial analysis to contract review.

🇮🇳 L3: Indic languages. Hindi, Hinglish, code-mixed text.

🧪 L4: Private golden set. Sealed tasks with planted traps, so scores can’t be gamed by memorized public data.

Not every skill has a benchmark, so we're honest about it:

✅ Public (120): a recognized benchmark exists
🟡 Proxy (34): only adjacent ones exist, so we add private tests
🛠️ Custom (13): nothing exists (SEO, pricing, due diligence), so we build it

Three rules we hold ourselves to:

- Success means pass^4: the task must work 4 times in a row, not once
- Every score ships with a 95% confidence interval, because “100% on 1 run” is noise
- The reviewer is never the worker

The result: when you hire an agent for a step, you know what it was actually tested on.
What’s the hardest agent skill to benchmark in your experience? I’d love to hear. 👇

The AI hiring tool is ready to ship, and nobody in the room is certain whose signature it needed.

Legal reviewed the contract. Security reviewed the vendor. The board saw a product update. Each assumed the oversight sat somewhere else.

This is where the distinction in Domain 1 does real work. Corporate governance is the system of practices that directs and controls a company, focused on stakeholder interests and accountability. AI governance is the set of frameworks, policies and processes guiding how AI is developed and deployed, so that it aligns with ethical standards, legal requirements and societal values.

They overlap. They are not substitutes. A company relying on corporate governance alone may never look inside the hiring algorithm, and the bias in it surfaces later as discriminatory practice, legal exposure and lost trust.

The gap is specialised oversight: diverse stakeholder input, regular audits of the system, explicit ownership of bias, transparency and accountability as standing questions rather than incident response.

So the useful exam question, and the useful meeting question, is the same one. Who owns this, and does the existing governance structure actually reach it?
